extracted.intended_audience: general readers interested in folklore, popular science, and lunar superstitions
extracted.subtask_description: Summarize and record traditional/folk and historical beliefs about the moon's effects on weather, health, birth, household practice, and ritual (as presented in a Victorian-era popular-science/folklore book).

rubrics_metrics.name: Mist-and-moon weather prognostications
rubrics_metrics.description: Proverbial rules linking mist plus moon phase to forthcoming rain or dry weather (e.g. 'An old moon in a mist / Is worth gold in a kist ... But a new moon's mist / Will never lack thirst'). Shepherd of Banbury rules: 'xii. If mists in the new moon, rain in the old.' 'xiii. If mists in the old, rain in the new moon.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multiple local variants cited (Cornwall, Banbury). Text notes regional sayings and juxtaposes contradictory forms; used as folk meteorology rather than scientific law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Full moon often indicates clear sky
rubrics_metrics.description: 'One thing is a meteorological certainty: the full moon very frequently clears the sky.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author adds the caveat that a full moon makes the night seem clear (moonlight reveals clarity that otherwise might be called cloudy), so observational bias may explain the proverb.

rubrics_metrics.name: 'Old moon in the arms of the new' and new-moon horn position as weather omen
rubrics_metrics.description: Seeing 'the old moon in the arms of the new one' and the 'turning up of the horns of the new moon' are reckoned signs of fair weather; horns turned down are thought to presage wet weather (folk idea that the moon 'retains water' when horns are up).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Southey anecdote and popular commentary show this as widespread popular explanation (also appears in ballads). Author treats it as imaginative folk theory (a 'novel idea of a lunar bason').

rubrics_metrics.name: Moon-plus-nearby-star/planet as storm prognostic ('a big star dogging the moon')
rubrics_metrics.description: Sailors and seafaring men believe that when a large star or planet is seen near the moon ('a big star is dogging the moon') this predicts wild weather; similar beliefs about 'moon dogs' (halos) meaning changing weather.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reported from Whitby, Ulceby, Devon fishermen; author notes strong faith among old sailors and that apparent proximity of moon and stars is optical, not causal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apparent star proximity to moon can be read as omen (local/cultural examples)
rubrics_metrics.description: Local anecdotes (Devon fisherman, Zulu account) interpret bright stars near the moon as omens (storms, war) based on cultural reading of celestial configurations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples used to illustrate cross-cultural tendency to read celestial occurences as portents; author emphasizes natural explanations (apparent proximity, atmospheric effects).

rubrics_metrics.name: Astrological doctrine: moon's natal influence on temperament, body, and fortune
rubrics_metrics.description: Astrology assigns the moon primary influence in nativities: zodiacal and mundane moon position and aspects to other planets determine success, health, sensations, moral tendencies, and physical traits. (Quoted: moon 'a cold, moist, watery, phlegmatic planet' producing 'full stature, fair, pale complexion, round face, gray eyes, short arms, thick hands and feet' and governing brain, stomach, bowels, left eye of male/right eye of female; usual diseases listed.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Long-established astrological system cited; author treats it critically but reports the content and lists diseases and bodily parts traditionally attributed to the moon. Useful as a statement of historical medical/astrological practice rather than evidence-based guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moon-phase effects on birth, child health, sex of next child, and development
rubrics_metrics.description: Folk beliefs that moon phase at birth or between birth and next events affects survival, mental state, sex of subsequent children, and robustness (e.g. 'children born between an old moon and the first appearance of a new one ... will never live to reach the age of puberty' and 'when a boy is born in the wane of the moon, it is believed that the next birth will be a girl, and vice versa').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited from Cornwall, Iceland, and broader European traditions; author notes persistence of such beliefs among both peasants and educated readers of historical authorities like Bacon.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weaning and child-care timed to moon phases
rubrics_metrics.description: Customs prescribing when to wean children according to moon phase (e.g. Scottish practice: avoid weaning during the wane; Lithuanian precept: wean boys at waxing, girls on a waning moon).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presented as common folk medical/customary practice across regions (Scotland, central Europe); author treats as superstition but documents prevalence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing of marriages and domestic/agricultural tasks by moon phase
rubrics_metrics.description: Full moon considered propitious for marriage (ancient Greeks); new moon pre-eminent for commencements (houses to be erected and moved into, marriages concluded, money counted, hair and nails cut, herbs gathered), while full moon is the time for pulling down, cutting timber, mowing grass, making hay, washing linen by the waning moon so dirt disappears.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lists many traditional domestic/agricultural prescriptions tied to waxing vs waning moon; author presents them as folk customs and proverbs (includes examples and the Earl of Northampton quotation about new garments).

rubrics_metrics.name: Household/financial superstitions tied to new moon (money luck etc.)
rubrics_metrics.description: Belief that money counted at the new moon will be increased; other household fortunes (e.g. assumption about new dress during decline of moon being unlucky) derive from lunar timing beliefs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Included among many proverbs about auspicious/inauspicious timing; author juxtaposes with Talmudic and Kabbalistic practices which ritualize the new moon.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ritual cures and therapeutic practices at change of moon
rubrics_metrics.description: Practices such as bringing infirm persons (rickety children) to bathe in a stream and dry in a cave 'at the change of the moon' as a cure; Staffordshire charm for 'chin-cough' performed looking at the new moon and reciting a formula while rubbing the child's stomach.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author records these as local folk remedies and ritual actions tied to lunar change; includes verbatim Staffordshire charm lines and Dunskey cave example as common ritual practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Medical/therapeutic scheduling by moon quadrant (phlebotomy and purging)
rubrics_metrics.description: La Martiniere and others advise timing bloodletting and purging according to moon quadrants: first quadrant warm and damp (bleed sanguine persons), second warm and dry (bleed choleric), third cold and moist (bleed phlegmatic), fourth cold and dry (bleed melancholic); Bacon recommends purging some days after the full moon.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Represents historical medical doctrine linking humoral theory to lunar phases; author cites these as reasons given historically for medical timing, not modern medical guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moonlight exposure believed to cause blindness or eye harm
rubrics_metrics.description: Accounts claiming that sleeping exposed to moonlight can impair or destroy sight (Egyptian/Arabian cautions, seaman avoiding facing full moon in hammock, stories of individuals who lost sight after sleeping outdoors on moonlit night).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author scrutinizes such claims, noting probable natural explanations (strong light on closed/slumbering eyes) and urges skepticism about attributing supernatural agency to moonlight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moon as cause or exacerbating factor in many diseases (lunacy, epilepsy, rheumatism, etc.)
rubrics_metrics.description: Traditional attribution of numerous maladies to lunar influence (apoplexy, paralysis, epilepsy, jaundice, hydropsy, lethargy, catalepsy, colds, convulsions, trembling, rheumatism, consumption, palsy, scrofula, smallpox, dropsy, etc.), and the label 'lunatic' from such beliefs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author traces these ideas historically (Pliny, Galen, Talmud references) and treats them as part of medical superstition that persisted into more recent centuries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Household grooming and minor surgical timing by moon phase (hair, nails, corns)
rubrics_metrics.description: Beliefs such as: cut hair and nails in the waning moon (beneficial); if corns are cut after the full moon they will gradually disappear; prosaic poem querying corns' growth related to moon's increase/decline.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recorded as common rural prescriptions (Devonshire, British Apollo); author presents examples and the popular verse to illustrate folk logic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moon-influenced fortune-telling and life-management practices (astrological lifestyle choices)
rubrics_metrics.description: Description of a superstitious person who times nearly all actions by lunar/planetary positions: when to cut hair (Leo/Aries), when to plant, when to take physic, when to seek a prince's presence (moon conjunct sun), avoid sea when Mars is high, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Satirical quotation used to show the extent of astrologically regulated life; author uses it to illustrate how pervasive such rubric-like prescriptions could be for believers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Blessing the new moon: ritual procedure and rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Detailed ritual guidance for 'Blessing the new moon': straighten the feet (as at Shemonah-esreh), give one glance at the moon before beginning the ritual blessing, and after commencing 'he should not look at her at all'; then proceed with the 'Form of Prayer for the New Moon' word for word, with solemn deliberation, repeating certain phrases and meditating on initials (three times).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Precise procedural directions quoted from the Kitzur Sh'lu (including the admonition about when and how to look at the moon), presented as prescriptive religious ritual rather than folk superstition.
